title: McLaren Vale Wine Show 2026 trophy winners revealed
summary:
The trophies from the 2026 MGA Insurance Group McLaren Vale Wine Show, including Best Wine of Show and the prestigious ‘Bushing Monarch’ title, were awarded at the 53rd annual McLaren Vale Bushing Lunch on Friday 30 October. The Big Easy Radio 2025 Perpetual Holidaze Grenache was named Best Wine of Show for 2026, crowning owner and winemaker Matt Head as the 2026 McLaren Vale Bushing Monarch. From 652 entries, the Big Easy Radio 2025 Perpetual Holidaze Grenache was awarded the highest accolade by the panel of judges including chair of judges Toby Barlow (Wine SX), international judge Richard Hemming MW (JancisRobinson.com) as well as panel chairs Glenn Barry (Tonic Wines), Steven Paul (Oakdene Vineyards) and Stuart Hordern (Brokenwood Wines).

content:
Big Easy Radio co-owners and ‘Bushing Monarchs’ Dr Bianca Price and Matt Head. Image credit Ben Macmahon

The trophies from the 2026 MGA Insurance Group McLaren Vale Wine Show, including Best Wine of Show and the prestigious ‘Bushing Monarch’ title, were awarded at the 53rd annual McLaren Vale Bushing Lunch on Friday 30 October.

The Big Easy Radio 2025 Perpetual Holidaze Grenache was named Best Wine of Show for 2026, crowning owner and winemaker Matt Head as the 2026 McLaren Vale Bushing Monarch.

From 652 entries, the Big Easy Radio 2025 Perpetual Holidaze Grenache was awarded the highest accolade by the panel of judges including chair of judges Toby Barlow (Wine SX), international judge Richard Hemming MW (JancisRobinson.com) as well as panel chairs Glenn Barry (Tonic Wines), Steven Paul (Oakdene Vineyards) and Stuart Hordern (Brokenwood Wines).

“Grenache was, as expected, a highlight and continues to be such an exciting and compelling story within Australian wine. However, the depth and expression across Shiraz wines also promoted a lot of discussion between judges and stiff competition for trophies. The standout trend in Shiraz was balance and freshness while sitting alongside Mclaren Vale’s trademark palate generosity,” said Barlow.

“This year’s show was also a poignant reminder of why this region continues to raise the bar for Mediterranean varieties in Australia. Many of the wines showed real confidence and varietal understanding from growers and winemakers in tune with their vineyard sites and climate.

The emerging varieties continue to positively develop across both red and whites and are becoming an integral part of the McLaren Vale narrative. The authentic fit between these varieties, their styles, the regional venues and outstanding food offering really elevates both the wine quality potential, but importantly the consumer experience too.”

Barlow emphasised that the Best Wine of Show vote was very close this year, however, the winning Grenache “just kept showing up and growing from the very first bracket”.

“It’s both modern and classic at the same time, and very compelling. On top of that every element was in balance, nothing out of place, with a finish that kept drawing the judges back. It captures McLaren Vale at its very best,” he concluded.

Visiting international judge Richard Hemming MW, head of creative, Asia for JancisRobinson.com, offered his global perspective to the judging.

“As expected, the Grenache, Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon wines were standouts, demonstrating the region’s aptitude for both compelling diversity and outstanding quality,” Hemming said.

He described his experience judging at the McLaren Vale Wine Show as “a seriously fun responsibility”.

“The work is no joke: hundreds of wines are scrutinised by multiple tasters in multiple stages to ensure that the very best efforts gain recognition. But the atmosphere is light-hearted, and the energy is nothing but positive. As an international judge, it was an honour to take part. And the results speak for themselves, demonstrating a level of excellence that makes McLaren Vale one of Australia’s most exciting and dynamic wine regions.”

McLaren Vale Wine Region CEO Erin Leggat reflected that the 2026 McLaren Vale Wine Show quality was exceptional.

“Around one in ten wines received a gold medal, with Grenache and Shiraz leading the field and varieties like Fiano and Nero d’Avola now standing up in their own right. These results confirm what trade and consumers increasingly know: McLaren Vale is producing some of the most distinctive and consistently high-quality wine in Australia.

“To see such depth across Shiraz, Grenache and our Mediterranean varieties, tells you this region isn’t standing still. Our growers and winemakers are refining what they do best and backing the varieties that suit our climate and our future,” Leggat said.

content:
Mercer Wines took home the top honour of 2026 Best Wine of Show. Images supplied

Last Friday, the 32nd edition of the NSW Wine Awards was held at the ICC Sydney.

The Hunter Valley’s Mercer Wines took home the top honour of 2026 Best Wine of Show with its 2025 Limited Release Chardonnay from Tumbarumba. Mercer Wines also picked up awards for Best Shiraz and Best Chardonnay, with both wines going on to win Best Red and White of Show respectively.

As is tradition, Aaron Mercer was presented with 2026 Best Wine of Show by Her Excellency the Honourable Margaret Beazley AC KC, Governor of NSW at ICC Sydney.

NSW is home to 16 distinct wine regions, with wines produced in all corners of the state taking home varietal and major trophies including three from Tumbarumba, two from Hilltops, one from Mudgee, three from Riverina, five from the Hunter Valley and six from Orange.

“It was a privilege to deep dive into NSW wine at the iconic ICC Sydney. The states wines and winemakers have continued to be recognised this year, and the wines tasted clearly showed that this recognition is deserving,” said chair of show Adam Walls.

“The Tumbarumba Chardonnay created real excitement amongst the judging team from the moment it was tasted on the bench. A high-quality Chardonnay that stands comfortably amongst the best in the country.”

With five gold medals and nine silver medals, First Creek Wines won Best Exhibitor of Show for the second year in a row.

Moreover, Angus Barnes was presented with the Graham Gregory Award by NSW Minister for Agriculture the Hon. Tara Moriarty MLC.

NSW Wine explained that the Graham Gregory Award is the industry’s highest accolade recognising individuals who have made outstanding and ongoing contribution to the NSW wine industry.

Barnes has served as executive officer of NSW Wine for five years, is chair of the wine committee at the Sydney Royal Wine Show, a board member and councillor of the Royal Agricultural Society of NSW, past executive chair and life member of the Wine Communicators of Australia and is also the 2025 recipient of the ‘Len Evans Prize’ for services to the Australian wine industry.

“For more than two decades, Angus has been a tireless advocate for the NSW and Australian wine industry, combining strategic leadership with a genuine commitment to supporting producers through both opportunity and adversity,” said Minister Moriarty.

“Mr Barnes achievements in these areas truly reflect the values of this award, and we are proud to celebrate his impact on both the local and national stages.”

Barnes said he is extremely grateful and proud to be named the recipient of the 2025 Graham Gregory Award.

“I have long looked at this award and the distinguished list of previous winners as a fantastic example of service to our great wine community in NSW. To join this list, which includes my father, Chris Barnes in 2013, is both a great honour and also a responsibility to uphold the high standards of service and contribution shown by these individuals.

“I love the NSW wine industry. We are vibrant and make wines that I like to drink. Challenges continue, but if we work together, sometimes for goals that focus on the collective rather than the individual, we will survive and thrive.

“Awards like these are given to an individual but are seldom achieved without the support of a community including my family, my employers, and good friends in the wine industry.”

Today, he continues to contribute to the local industry, working as general manager of Bunnamagoo Estate Wines and serving as a Mudgee Wine Association board member.

“On behalf of the NSW Wine Industry, I congratulate Angus Barnes on receiving the 2025 Graham Gregory Award,” said NSW Wine president Mark Bourne.

“This year’s award is also a first in its history. Angus joins his father, Chris, who received the award in 2013, making them the first father and son to be recognised. It reflects a family commitment to the NSW wine industry spanning generations, and the values of service and leadership that Graham Gregory himself championed. I congratulate Angus and the Barnes family on this remarkable achievement.”

The Graham Gregory Award is named in honour of the former NSW Agriculture Deputy Director General “who was instrumental in the development of the NSW wine industry”.

summary:

content:
First Ridge co-owner and vigneron John Nicholas explained there is renewed enthusiasm for Italian wines. Images supplied

First Ridge Wines has released two new vintage red wines — the 2024 First Ridge Montepulciano and the 2024 First Ridge Barbera — to embrace the Mudgee region’s Italian wine heritage amid increased curiosity surrounding alternative varieties.

“For more than 165 years, Mudgee has been growing grapes and making wine. It is one of the pioneering wine regions of NSW,” said First Ridge co-owner and vigneron John Nicholas.

“In the 60s and 70s, the region was reinvigorated, with new winemakers establishing vineyards and wine brands. Many of these vineyards are still producing great wines.

“Today, there is a real willingness to experiment with varieties and winemaking techniques. The increasing popularity of Italian and other ‘alternative’ varieties shows how the region’s success stems from innovations that complement its historic vineyards.

“While Italian varieties are certainly not new to Mudgee, with Italian winemaker Carlo Corino championing varieties such as Barbera, Sangiovese and Nebbiolo at Montrose in the 1970s, there is a renewed enthusiasm for them, supported by the demand we are seeing in the Sydney market.”

The winery explained that the 2024 Mudgee vintage was characterised by a dry winter and early spring, followed by useful November rainfall and a warm, sunny summer, resulting in an earlier-than-usual harvest.

“Relatively low disease pressure allowed First Ridge to maintain healthy fruit and focus on quality. The Montepulciano and Barbera produced fruit with good colour, freshness and balance,” it added.

First Ridge said that both wines were made in a similar manner, with the objective of allowing the fruit to shine. The grapes were crushed into small fermenters, cold-soaked for 48 hours and then inoculated. Moderate fermentation temperatures of around 22–24°C were maintained, with twice-daily pump-overs to extract colour and build depth of flavour.

“We have recently partnered with Clarity Cru to distribute our wines in Sydney,” said Nicholas.

“The response and take-up of the wines has been very promising, showing that these Italian varieties, grown in NSW’s Mudgee region, have a place on the wine lists of Sydney’s restaurants and cafés.”

The wines retail for $45 each and are distributed in NSW by Clarity Cru or available directly from the winery’s website.

title: Mark Harvey-Sutton announced as new Australian Grape & Wine CEO
summary:
Australian Grape & Wine (AGW) has today announced the appointment of Mark Harvey-Sutton as its new CEO, bringing “extensive experience in industry leadership, agricultural trade and national advocacy” to the role. Harvey-Sutton has served as CEO of the Australian Livestock Exporters' Council since 2019, representing Australian exporters on international trade, market access and regulatory matters. He previously held senior roles with the National Farmers' Federation, other agricultural organisations and the Australian Government. AGW board chair Helen Strachan welcomed the appointment, saying Harvey-Sutton's experience would bring a fresh perspective to the organisation.

The post Mark Harvey-Sutton announced as new Australian Grape & Wine CEO appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
Mark Harvey-Sutton will commence as CEO of AGW on 13 January 2027. Image supplied

Australian Grape & Wine (AGW) has today announced the appointment of Mark Harvey-Sutton as its new CEO, bringing “extensive experience in industry leadership, agricultural trade and national advocacy” to the role.

Harvey-Sutton has served as CEO of the Australian Livestock Exporters’ Council since 2019, representing Australian exporters on international trade, market access and regulatory matters. He previously held senior roles with the National Farmers’ Federation, other agricultural organisations and the Australian Government.

AGW board chair Helen Strachan welcomed the appointment, saying Harvey-Sutton’s experience would bring a fresh perspective to the organisation.

“Mark brings an impressive combination of industry leadership, policy expertise and experience representing Australian agricultural exporters at the highest levels of government,” Strachan said.

“His understanding of international trade and market access will be particularly valuable as we look to build new opportunities for Australian wine at home and abroad.

“Mark’s appointment marks an exciting new chapter for AGW. We look forward to strengthening our engagement with members, building industry collaboration and ensuring AGW remains a strong, effective voice for Australian grapegrowers and winemakers.”

Harvey-Sutton said he was excited to take on the role and looked forward to working with members and stakeholders across the industry.

“Australia’s grape and wine industry has an outstanding international reputation and makes an enormous contribution to our economy and regional communities,” he said.

“There are significant opportunities to build on the industry’s strengths and position Australian grapegrowers and winemakers for the future.

“I’m looking forward to getting out into the regions, listening to members and working collaboratively to ensure AGW delivers strong advocacy and practical outcomes for the businesses it represents.”

He will commence as CEO on 13 January 2027.

content:
Winemaker Nyall Condon of Jack Rabbit Vineyard pictured with the trophy. Image supplied

Victoria’s Jack Rabbit Vineyard has come out on top at the 2026 Saint Martin Oak Great Australian Shiraz Challenge, winning the ‘Best Shiraz of Show Trophy’ as well as the ‘Sanector Trophy for Best Victorian Shiraz’ with its 2025 Jack Rabbit Vineyard Shiraz.

“Jack Rabbit Vineyard has triumphed in 2026, this is the first time a wine from the Bellarine Peninsula has won the coveted Best Shiraz of Show Trophy,” said event director Julian McLean.

This year’s event marks the 32nd edition of the challenge and garnered support from a total of 49 regions across the country. Organisers noted fierce competition particularly from the McLaren Vale, Barossa Valley and Margret River regions.

Other significant accolades included Peter Lehmann Wines taking out the ‘Interpack Trophy for Best Sparkling Shiraz’ with the 2021 The Queen Shiraz, having also won back in 2023 and 2024. Tamburlaine Vineyard also took home the ‘MCC Labels Best NSW Shiraz Trophy’ for a second year running, this time with their 2025 Tamburlaine Point 65 Single Vineyard Shiraz.

Additional trophies awarded are as follows:

  • Orora Glass Best South Australian Shiraz: 2024 Hentley Farm “The Beast” Shiraz
  • Melbourne Royal Best Organic Shiraz: 2024 Yangarra Estate Shiraz
  • Sanector Best Tasmanian Shiraz: 2024 Pooley Wines Syrah
  • Winetitles Best Western Australia Shiraz: 2024 Mandoon Estate Old Vine Shiraz
  • Sanector Best Victorian Shiraz: 2025 Jack Rabbit Vineyard Shiraz
  • Hahn Corporation Best Shiraz over 5 years old: Thorn -Clarke 2021 William Randell Shiraz

The 2026 judging panel involved Jen Pfeiffer (chair), Liz Heidenreich, Tyson Bitter, Steve Paul, Justin Purser and Brendan Freeman.

Organisers said that, nationally, there are considerably more Shiraz plantings than any other red varietal, and that the “challenge for Australian Winemakers is to effectively promote this iconic variety”. They highlighted that the challenge has played an important role in this by “raising industry, press and consumer awareness of Shiraz, both nationally and internationally” for the past 32 years.

content:
More than 500 wines were judges over three days. Image credit Richard Briggs

70 wines were awarded gold at the 2026 Marlborough Wine Show with chief judge Stu Marfell saying the results show a wine region in fine form.

Judges spent three days tasting more than 500 wines last week, awarding 70 gold, 140 silver and 180 bronze medals in total.

Sauvignon Blanc (Current Vintage) and Chardonnay (Current Vintage) were the leading categories, picking up 19 and 12 gold medals respectively.

“It’s been exciting, we’ve had another strong vintage with the 2026’s,” Marfell said.

“Aromatics and Sauvignon Blancs have been really strong, and it’s been cool to see things like Albariño performing. It’s a wine that has got so much personality and potential, so that’s pretty fun.”

“There’s a lot for Marlborough to be proud of, there really are some great wines coming through, and it’s pretty exciting. There’s a lot to like for wine drinkers, across everything from Albariño to Pinot Noir and everything in between, they are all looking really good.”

The quality of 2026 followed two strong vintages in 2024 and 2025, Marfell said. He added that tasting the Legacy entries, which included three vintages of the same wine from within a 10-year period, further proved that some Marlborough wines get even better with age.

“We’re probably almost drinking [these wines] a bit young, at times. There were some really great older wines, and sometimes, of the three wines, it was the oldest of the three that really shone through as being the most interesting.”

Marfell was joined for the tasting by shadow chief judge, Marlborough winemaker Murray Cook; guest judge Jennifer Docherty MW from Hong Kong; New Zealand-based Terry Copeland; and a team of senior as well as associate judges.

“Jennifer and Terry were both amazing to have on the team, bringing both knowledge and enthusiasm — and we’ve had some new associates and judges stepping into senior roles as well this year, so it’s really nice to see that progression coming through. It’s also been great to have Murray in the shadow chief role. He has a great focus on the wines and brings fresh ideas to the show.”

Marfell will shadow Murray Cook as he steps into the role of chief judge in 2027.

This year’s medal winners were notified of their success yesterday at 12pm. Trophies will be announced at the 2026 Marlborough Wine Show Celebration, this year taking place on Friday 13 November at the Queen Charlotte Yacht Club in Picton.

Two Wine Marlborough Lifetime Achievement Award recipients will also be announced at the celebration.

title: Australian sommeliers selected to receive New Zealand Wine scholarship
summary:
New Zealand Winegrowers and Sommeliers Australia have announced Alexander Jacques of New South Wales and Russ Wilcox of Victoria as the Australian recipients of the 2027 New Zealand Wine Sommelier Scholarship. The selected scholars will join an international cohort of wine professionals from New Zealand, Asia, Canada, the UK and the USA for an “immersive exploration of New Zealand wine”, beginning with Sommit in the Waitaki Valley on 22–23 January 2027 hosted by New Zealand wine experts Cameron Douglas MS and Stephen Wong MW. The New Zealand Wine Sommelier Scholarship, first launched in association with Sommeliers Australia in 2015, has since grown into a global initiative. It is designed to allow passionate wine professionals to connect with the landscapes, varieties and personalities that make New Zealand wine distinctively unique.

content:
LTR: Alex Jacques and Russ Wilcox. Images supplied

New Zealand Winegrowers and Sommeliers Australia have announced Alexander Jacques of New South Wales and Russ Wilcox of Victoria as the Australian recipients of the 2027 New Zealand Wine Sommelier Scholarship.

The selected scholars will join an international cohort of wine professionals from New Zealand, Asia, Canada, the UK and the USA for an “immersive exploration of New Zealand wine”, beginning with Sommit in the Waitaki Valley on 22–23 January 2027 hosted by New Zealand wine experts Cameron Douglas MS and Stephen Wong MW.

The New Zealand Wine Sommelier Scholarship, first launched in association with Sommeliers Australia in 2015, has since grown into a global initiative. It is designed to allow passionate wine professionals to connect with the landscapes, varieties and personalities that make New Zealand wine distinctively unique.

Catherine Wansink, Australia market consultant at New Zealand Winegrowers, emphasised the importance of this initiative.

“We are entering the next chapter of the New Zealand wine story, and the Sommit experience is a deep immersion into what that looks like.  Alex and Russ will be well placed to share back and be part of the storytelling in their Australian wine communities upon their return. As well as having a sensational New Zealand wine experience.”

Sommeliers Australia spokesperson Alicia Noble said the organisation is proud of its longstanding partnership with New Zealand Winegrowers.

“The Sommelier Scholarship and Sommit programme create invaluable opportunities for Australian wine professionals to build their knowledge, develop industry connections and experience New Zealand wine at its source.

“Congratulations to Alex and Russ, our 2027 recipients. We’re excited for them to explore New Zealand’s diverse wine regions, meet the people behind the wines and bring those insights back to their peers and the wider Australian wine community.”

About the recipients

Alexander Jacques is a Sydney-based sommelier and head of wine operations at 67 Pall Mall Sydney. His current role spans procurement strategy, team management and overseeing the expansion of the global group into Australia. His career spans some of the world’s most respected dining rooms; including Quay and Bennelong in Sydney, as well as Copenhagen’s Restaurant Geranium, which was crowned the best in the world in 2022 by The World’s 50 Best Restaurants. The domestic wine judge and master sommelier candidate said he looks forward to soaking up as much as he can in beautiful New Zealand.

Russ Wilcox is a Melbourne-based sommelier and head sommelier at Rodd & Gunn’s hospitality flagship, The Lodge. Originally from Aotearoa New Zealand, he has worked across front of house and beverage-focused roles, most recently at Gimlet in Melbourne and Ahi in Auckland. Drawing on his deep knowledge of New Zealand wine, Russ’s current position involves procurement, team training and mentorship, and bringing lesser-known New Zealand wineries and regions to the forefront of the beverage programme. He said he looks forward to continuing to build his knowledge and relationships within the New Zealand wine industry.

Following Sommit, the recipients will travel to Central Otago and Wairarapa, before concluding their New Zealand experience at Sauvignon Blanc New Zealand in Marlborough from 2–4 February. Through the event and additional regional experiences, they will build a deeper understanding of New Zealand’s flagship variety and the wider diversity of the country’s wine offering.

title: Why Independent Wine Retailers Still Matter
summary:
For Australian winemakers, getting a bottle onto a shelf is only part of the challenge. What happens next can be just as important. Who is there to explain what makes that wine different? The post Why Independent Wine Retailers Still Matter appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
For Australian winemakers, getting a bottle onto a shelf is only part of the challenge. What happens next can be just as important.

Who is there to explain what makes that wine different? Who can suggest the right bottle for a particular meal, occasion or budget? And who can convince a customer to try an unfamiliar producer instead of reaching for the label they already know? In an increasingly consolidated retail market, that personal connection still gives independent wine retailers an important role.

Large retail networks are naturally built around scale, consistency and national distribution. Independent retailers operate differently. They can tailor their ranges to local customers, work closely with suppliers and producers, and give smaller or less familiar labels the opportunity to sit alongside established names.

Bayfield’s Liquor Superstores on Sydney’s Northern Beaches is one example of that model in practice. The independent retailer currently carries more than 1,200 wines, spanning Australian and international producers, established favourites and lesser-known discoveries across a broad range of regions, varieties and price points.

Choice beyond the familiar

Buying wine can quickly become overwhelming.

Even regular wine drinkers often return to a familiar handful of varieties, regions or brands. Yet the diversity of Australian wine extends well beyond the labels most customers immediately recognise.

Independent retailers can help bridge that gap.

A broad range creates room for smaller Australian producers, emerging wine regions, alternative varieties and selected imports that may not receive the same exposure in larger, more standardised retail networks.

For smaller wineries without large marketing budgets or national brand recognition, that opportunity can be particularly valuable.

Getting a wine onto a shelf is one thing. Having it stocked somewhere that staff understand the product, know where it comes from and can explain why a customer might enjoy it is another.

Independent retailers can also respond quickly to the preferences of their own customers. If local drinkers start showing more interest in a particular region, style or variety, buyers have the ability to adjust the range without every decision needing to suit stores across the country.

At Bayfield’s, wine buying and ranging is handled internally by long-standing product buyers Andy and Chris.

Their role is not simply to build a large range, but to balance the wines customers already know with products that give them an opportunity to try something different.

“For us, it’s about giving customers genuine choice and the chance to discover something new,” the Bayfield’s team said.

“We want everything from familiar favourites to different producers, regions and varieties, across a range of price points. And just as importantly, we’ve got a team who know the range and can help customers find something they’ll really enjoy.”

The counter conversation

That conversation remains one of the most valuable parts of independent wine retail.

Someone buying a case of their regular beer may know exactly what they want before they enter the store. Wine purchases are often less straightforward.

A customer might be looking for an easy midweek red, a bottle for a dinner party, a gift for someone with different tastes, or simply an alternative to a wine they already enjoy.

A shelf ticket can provide basic information, but it cannot always answer those questions.

A knowledgeable staff member can take a broad request and turn it into a useful recommendation. That might mean suggesting a different producer from a familiar region, introducing a customer to a variety they have not tried before, or simply finding the best option within a particular budget.

For producers, that interaction matters.

A smaller winery may not have the advertising spend or brand recognition needed to catch a shopper’s attention from across the store. A recommendation from someone the customer trusts can help overcome that barrier.

In that sense, knowledgeable retail staff can become an important connection between producer and consumer.

Range needs curation, not just scale

Carrying more than 1,200 wines gives Bayfield’s considerable breadth, but a large range only works when there is purpose behind it.

Customers shop for wine for very different reasons.

One might be looking for an affordable bottle for a Tuesday night dinner. Another may want Champagne for a celebration. Someone else may be searching for a premium Australian red, a particular region, or simply something new to try.

A well-curated independent range needs to cater for all of those customers across different price points, regions and styles.

It also creates room for discovery within familiar categories.

A customer looking for Shiraz does not necessarily need to leave with the same nationally recognised label every time. A retailer with depth in the category can suggest another producer, region or style at a similar price point.

That gives customers more choice while creating opportunities for producers that may otherwise be difficult to discover.

Importantly, a broad range also gives independent buyers more freedom to take chances.

Not every wine needs to appeal to every shopper. A smaller allocation from an emerging producer or a less familiar region can still find the right audience when the retailer understands both the product and its customers.

An important route to market

Australia’s wine retail landscape will continue to include major national groups, and those businesses play an important role in providing scale and distribution.

Independent retailers serve a different purpose.

They can provide another route to market for producers, offer space to wines that do not necessarily fit a high-volume retail model, and respond to the particular tastes of their local customers.

They can also help make a complex category easier to navigate.

For Bayfield’s, maintaining a range of more than 1,200 wines is not simply about offering more bottles. It is about combining breadth of choice with staff knowledge, local buying decisions and the opportunity for customers to discover something they may not have found otherwise.

For producers, especially smaller and independent wineries, retailers willing to understand, recommend and advocate for those wines remain an important part of the route to the consumer.

In a crowded market where getting noticed can be as difficult as producing the wine itself, that role still matters.

title: China remains SA wine’s biggest export market as trade mission heads to Shanghai

The post China remains SA wine’s biggest export market as trade mission heads to Shanghai appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
Mainland China was worth $632 million in South Australian wine exports in the year to September 2026, ahead of a state government trade mission to China aimed at strengthening export relationships.

Led by Primary Industries and Regional Development Minister Clare Scriven, the delegation will visit Jinan, Weifang, Qingdao and Shanghai over a week. South Australian wine, seafood, honey and beverage producers will take part in a Taste of South Australia event ahead of the China International Import Expo in Shanghai, connecting with Chinese importers and distributors.

China is also South Australia’s largest export market for primary industries. Exports grew 26% to nearly $1.9 billion in the year to August 2026, accounting for 23% of the state’s total agricultural, food, wine and forestry export value.

Wine Australia data shows Chinese consumers are spending more on South Australian Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay and Riesling.

The visit coincides with the 40th anniversary of the sister-state relationship between South Australia and China’s Shandong province. The delegation will also progress priorities under the South Australia–Shandong Food, Wine and Agribusiness Working Group.

Minister Scriven and her delegation will discuss further cooperation between the Shandong Academy of Agricultural Sciences and South Australia’s Department of Primary Industries and Regions. This includes the Wine Industry Technical Collaboration Program and potential future work in cropping, soil science, horticulture and animal husbandry.

“China remains a vital market for South Australian producers, which is why I am leading a delegation to help strengthen trade relationships and unlock new export opportunities,” Minister Scriven said.

“Our premium food, wine, seafood and beverages are highly regarded internationally, and we are proud to be able to showcase them at one of the world’s biggest trade exhibitions in the China International Import Expo.”
